messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 54, Elena Martin came to treatment exhausted by the sense that danger had followed her into every ordinary part of her life. She was a married woman who had spent most of her adult life working as a chef, used to the pressure and noise of a professional kitchen, but the assault that changed her had happened not in some obviously dangerous place but after work with a man she had trusted. She still struggled to describe it directly. When she tried, the story broke apart into flashes: the shift ending late, a conversation that turned personal, being alone with him, the sudden realization that she was no longer safe. What remained strongest was not a clear sequence but the physical memory of it. Even now, when it came back, her body would tense and fold into the same position she had been in then, as if she were back inside the moment before she had words for it.

In the months afterward, Elena found that certain conversation topics could undo her almost instantly. If coworkers drifted into talk about relationships, trust, or men who had “crossed a line,” she would go still and lose the thread of the present. The memory did not return as a coherent account. It came in disconnected pieces and bodily sensations she could not organize, and her inability to put the event into words frightened her in its own right. Those same moments also sharpened what she had come to believe about people: that someone she had trusted had betrayed her, that people could not be trusted, that there was no reliable way to know who would harm you until it was too late.

That betrayal became the lens through which she moved through the world. Elena had come to believe that trust itself was dangerous, and from there it made sense to her to stay guarded. In the restaurant, if a male supplier arrived early and she found herself briefly alone with him near the walk-in refrigerator, her chest tightened before anything even happened. If one of the line cooks stepped too close behind her at the stove, she reacted before she could think, jolting hard at the movement. She told herself this vigilance was necessary because strangers approaching in ordinary situations did not feel ordinary anymore; they felt like potential threats. The more convinced she became that anyone might cause harm, the more watchful she stayed, scanning doorways, footsteps, and shifts in tone.

That same way of seeing people also made her triggers spread. Emotional closeness became especially difficult. When her husband tried to ask what she was going through or reached for her in a tender, concerned way, she did not experience it simply as comfort. Being known too closely stirred the same conviction that trust led to betrayal, and she would pull back, change the subject, or leave the room. Even certain kinds of conversation now felt dangerous before they began, because she anticipated where they might lead inside her own mind. She was not just reacting to reminders; she had started to brace against them in advance.

Her constant alertness fed the memories too. In the kitchen, unexpected movement in the corner of her eye could make her heart slam and her muscles lock, and in that split second her body seemed to remember before she did. The feeling of being under threat brought back the assault as posture, tension, and scattered images, not as narrative. Afterward she was left with the same terrible conclusion: if her body reacted this quickly, it proved to her that the world really was unsafe and that her distrust was justified. Those fragmented returns to the event deepened her certainty that she had been betrayed in a fundamental way and that no one was reliably safe.

The memories themselves kept those beliefs alive. Because they arrived in pieces she could not fully explain, Elena felt she could never get enough distance from what happened to make sense of it. What frightened her most was that the assault seemed to live on outside words, in her body, as if it could happen again at any moment. That made her mistrust feel less like an opinion than like knowledge. And once she was on guard, she noticed men more quickly, strangers more sharply, certain topics more immediately, as though her whole system had learned to pick out what might expose her again.

By the time she sought help, the pattern had narrowed her life. At work she arranged prep tasks to avoid being alone with male coworkers. At home she kept her husband at an emotional distance that pained them both. She finally came in after snapping at a server who had approached her unexpectedly from behind and then spending the rest of the night shaken by bodily flashes of the assault she could not explain. Elena said she was afraid that if she let her guard down, she would be harmed again by someone she should have known better than to trust. What she hoped for, cautiously, was not to become naive, but to be able to stand in her own kitchen, hear ordinary conversation, and feel that her body belonged in the present again.
